ety.text: Latin vectorlbor. English vector Learned borrowing from Latin vector (“carrier, transporter”), from vehō (“to carry, transport, bear”), also ultimately the root of English vehicle. The “person or entity that passes along an urban legend or other meme” sense derives from the disease sense. The mathematics sense was coined by Irish mathematician and astronomer William Rowan Hamilton in 1846.

senses.d: A directed quantity, one with both magnitude and direction; the signed difference between two points.
ex: Velocity is a vector defined by the speed of an object and its direction.

senses.d: Any member of a (generalized) vector space.
An ordered tuple, originally one representing a directed quantity, but by extension any one-dimensional matrix.
ex: Computers store many types of data as vectors for ease of processing.
Color is stored as a vector attribute (R, G, B).

senses.d: A chosen course or direction for motion, as of an aircraft.
ex: I was told to fly out on a vector of 100 degrees to meet a strong plot of aircraft 30 miles from the coast.

senses.d: A kind of dynamically resizable array.
ex: To create a vector of students in a class, you will want the vector to be large enough […]

senses.d: A memory address containing the address of a code entry point, usually one which is part of a table and often one that is dereferenced and jumped to during the execution of an interrupt.
A graphical representation using outlines; vector graphics.
A DNA molecule used to carry genetic information from one organism into another.
A person or entity that passes along an urban legend or other meme.
A recurring psychosocial issue that stimulates growth and development in the personality.
To set (particularly an aircraft) on a course toward a selected point.
ex: […] if love is vectored toward an object and Elinor's here flies toward Marianne, Marianne's in turn toward Willoughby.

senses.d: To redirect to a vector, or code entry point.

grp.label: aviation: chosen course or direction for motion
